catalog_quote: — p. 89 (§31.42). On the basis of data from the other languages, Arabic in particular, the rule for accent in a word containing no long vowels is not that the accent is on the first syllable, but that it is on the third syllable from the end of the word unless a long vowel intervenes, in which case the syllable containing that vowel takes the accent. [p. 61] ... Certainly in the /YQTLØ/ and plausibly in the imperative of the derived stems, where the accent would not have been on the final syllable because one of the preceding syllables was long (e.g., /ḥáwwi/), I see no reason to doubt that the Ugaritic pattern was similar to that of Arabic. [p. 318] ||| Tropper 2000 §31.4 (snippet fragments, German): ... das Ar. und die äthiosem. Sprachen einen mechanischen Akzent; lediglich im He. hat der Akzent sporadisch phonemischen Wert. Im Akk. gelten folgende Akzentregeln: a) der Akzent liegt nur dann auf der letzten Silbe (Ultima), wenn diese einen Kontraktionsvokal enhält, der auf einen Triphthong zurückgeht. b) Ansonsten wandert der Akzent so weit von der Ultima [p. 89] nach vor, bis er auf eine lange Silbe trifft. c) Gibt es keine lange Silbe im Wort, wird die erste Silbe des Wortes betont ... einen nicht-phonemischen Akzent besaß. Die Akzentregeln dürften denen des Akk. entsprechen.

On the basis of data from the other languages, Arabic in particular, the rule for accent in a word containing no long vowels is not that the accent is on the first syllable, but that it is on the third syllable from the end of the word unless a long vowel intervenes, in which case…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ugaritic is written without vowels, so word stress is reconstructed, not observed. Tropper (2000, §31.4 Wortakzent, pp. 88-89) is reported to put the accent on the first syllable when the word has no long vowel, otherwise on the syllable with the long vowel. Pardee counters with an Arabic-type rule: accent on the antepenult unless a long vowel intervenes, in which case that long-vowel syllable is stressed; on p. 320 he adds that the accent was not on the final syllable when a preceding syllable was long (e.g. /ḥáwwi/). A third view (Zevit 1983, snippet only) puts nondistinctive main stress on the penult of bisyllabic words. All are hypotheses; none is confirmed by the script.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not addressed by Pardee/Tropper. Zevit 1983 (snippet only) posits secondary stress on every second syllable from the main stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Pardee p. 215: the accent of the 2 f.s. imperative is left open (final as in Hebrew vs. penultimate as in Aramaic); Schniedewind & Hunt 2007 p. 76 (snippet) suggest the jussive was distinguished from the indicative by stress retracted to the first syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level accent of reconstructed vocalized forms (citation forms with case/mood endings); the language is extinct and unvocalized, so all statements are comparative reconstructions and mutually contradictory (initial vs. antepenult/long-vowel vs. penult).
new_statements.identity_note: Ugaritic (ugar1238, ISO uga), extinct Northwest Semitic language of Ugarit (Ras Shamra, Syria), 14th-12th c. BCE, written in a consonantal cuneiform alphabet; stress is never written, so every statement is a comparative reconstruction. The Glottolog country code IL is wrong for the site (Syria).

sources.locator: review p. 61 (online version), remark to Tropper 2000 p. 89 (§31.42); cf. p. 320 and p. 215
sources.note: Remark to Tropper p. 89 (§31.42), review p. 61: reports Tropper's rule that in a word with no long vowels the accent is on the first syllable and counters that (on Arabic evidence) it falls on the third syllable from the end unless a long vowel intervenes, in which case the long-vowel syllable is accented; p. 320 repeats that the accent is not on the final syllable when a preceding syllable is long, assuming an Arabic-like pattern; p. 215 notes Tropper never addresses whether the 2 f.s. imperative was accented finally (as Hebrew) or penultimately (as Aramaic).

sources.quote: Ugaritic exhibits three syllable types: CV̆ (open syllable with short vowel) / CV̄ (i.e., CVː, open syllable with long vowel) / CV̌C (closed syllable with short vowel). Lengthened (geminated) consonants are spread over two syllables: /kak.ka.ru/ 'talent'. The question of whether Ugaritic had phonemic stress cannot be decided with certainty. Comparative evidence, however, suggests that stress was not phonemic, that is, that it was mechanically assigned by rule.
sources.note: Most recent authoritative sketch by the author of the reference grammar; phonology section may restate the §31.4 accent rule in English.
